steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on adversarial attacks against the fairness of graph neural networks: motivate why fairness attacks matter, explain what makes them harder than ordinary attacks, and summarize our attack method and contributions.

steps.text:
## Introduction
- GNNs successful in human-centered applications

  - fairness-aware GNNs: learn fair node representations for accurate + fair predictions
  - strategies: adversarial training, regularization, edge rewiring
- Fairness can be corrupted by malicious attackers
  - attacks perturb input graph data -> unfair predictions
  - compromises reliability even with built-in fairness mechanism
  - example: GNN-based recommender in social networks; commercial competition / personal benefits
  - adversary hijacks inactive user accounts, collects data, trains fairness attack model
  - modifies attributes + connections of compromised accounts -> biased predictions against a user group
- Our problem: adversarial attacks on fairness of GNNs
  - need to understand attack routes before protecting
  - most existing studies attack utility (e.g., prediction accuracy) only
  - formulate attack as optimization; gray-box setting (no access to victim architecture/parameters)
  - common strategy: train a surrogate model
  - challenge 1: surrogate loss design; prior utility attacks use cross-entropy (CE); fairness-aware GNNs use demographic parity loss, mutual information loss, Wasserstein distance loss; victim unknown
  - challenge 2: unnoticeability; owner may take defensive actions (e.g., abandon poisoned data); usually restrict perturbation size; distinct utility change is also a clue; not considered by existing fairness attacks
- G-FairAttack: surrogate loss + optimization method
  - categorize fairness-aware GNNs into three types by fairness loss terms
  - novel surrogate loss with theoretical analysis
  - unnoticeable constraint in utility change
  - non-gradient attack algorithm, better than gradient-based methods
  - fast computation strategy for scalability
- Contributions
  - Attack Setting: unnoticeable constraint on utility change; extends to general fairness attacks
  - Objective Design: surrogate loss for various fairness-aware GNNs
  - Algorithmic Design: deficiency of gradient-based methods; non-gradient method; fast computation lowers time complexity
  - Experimental Evaluation: three real-world datasets, four types of victim models; fairness jeopardized, unnoticeable utility effect

steps.text:
## Introduction

GNNs (Graph Neural Networks) have been very successful in a lot of human-centered applications, for example social network analysis, recommender systems, and healthcare. But many recent studies showed that GNNs can give biased predictions for nodes from some demographic groups (e.g., females). Since GNNs are becoming more important in high-stakes human-centered scenarios, it is imperative to address this prediction bias. So a lot of effort has gone into developing fairness-aware GNNs, which aim to learn fair node representations that can be used to make predictions that are accurate and fair. Typical strategies to make GNNs fairer are adversarial training, regularization, and edge rewiring.

These fairness-aware GNN frameworks can make fair predictions, but there is a high risk that their fairness gets corrupted by malicious attackers. Adversarial attacks perturb the input graph data and this threatens the fairness of the victim model, so it makes unfair predictions. Such fairness attacks can severely compromise how reliable GNNs are, even when the GNNs have a fairness-enhancing mechanism built in. As an example, consider a GNN-based recommender system in social networks. For commercial competition or personal benefits, a malicious adversary might hijack inactive user accounts to conduct fairness attacks. The adversary can collect user data from these accounts and use it to train a fairness attack model. Then, following the fairness attack algorithm, the adversary can modify the attributes and connections of these compromised accounts. As a result the GNN-based system gets the poisoned input data and makes biased predictions against a specific user group.

- To protect fairness, first understand how fairness can be attacked -> we study adversarial attacks on fairness of GNNs
  - most existing studies only attack utility (e.g., prediction accuracy)
  - optimization formulation, gray-box setting, surrogate model
  - challenge 1: surrogate loss (CE vs. demographic parity / mutual information / Wasserstein distance losses; victim unknown)
  - challenge 2: unnoticeable attacks; utility change is also a clue; ignored so far
- G-FairAttack: surrogate loss + optimization method
  - three types of fairness-aware GNNs; novel surrogate loss with theory
  - unnoticeable constraint in utility change; non-gradient algorithm; fast computation
- Contributions: attack setting, objective design, algorithmic design, experimental evaluation (three datasets, four types of victim models)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

GNNs (Graph Neural Networks) have been very successful in a lot of human-centered applications, for example social network analysis, recommender systems, and healthcare. But many recent studies showed that GNNs can give biased predictions for nodes from some demographic groups (e.g., females). Since GNNs are becoming more important in high-stakes human-centered scenarios, it is imperative to address this prediction bias. So a lot of effort has gone into developing fairness-aware GNNs, which aim to learn fair node representations that can be used to make predictions that are accurate and fair. Typical strategies to make GNNs fairer are adversarial training, regularization, and edge rewiring.

These fairness-aware GNN frameworks can make fair predictions, but there is a high risk that their fairness gets corrupted by malicious attackers. Adversarial attacks perturb the input graph data and this threatens the fairness of the victim model, so it makes unfair predictions. Such fairness attacks can severely compromise how reliable GNNs are, even when the GNNs have a fairness-enhancing mechanism built in. As an example, consider a GNN-based recommender system in social networks. For commercial competition or personal benefits, a malicious adversary might hijack inactive user accounts to conduct fairness attacks. The adversary can collect user data from these accounts and use it to train a fairness attack model. Then, following the fairness attack algorithm, the adversary can modify the attributes and connections of these compromised accounts. As a result the GNN-based system gets the poisoned input data and makes biased predictions against a specific user group.

To protect the fairness of GNN models from adversarial attacks, we first need to fully understand the potential ways fairness can be attacked. So in this paper we investigate the problem of adversarial attacks on fairness of GNNs. Even though it is important to investigate fairness attacks on GNNs, most existing studies only focus on attacking the utility of GNNs (e.g., prediction accuracy) and they neglect the vulnerability of GNNs in terms of fairness. To study fairness attacks, we follow existing works on attacks on GNNs and formulate the attack as an optimization problem, and we consider the gray-box attack setting which is prevalent, where the attacker cannot access the architecture or parameters of the victim model. In gray-box attacks a common strategy is to train a surrogate model to get more knowledge about the unseen victim model for the attack. Our attack on fairness is more difficult than conventional adversarial attacks because of two challenges. (1) How to design the surrogate loss function. Previous attacks on prediction utility just choose the loss function that most victim models use, i.e. the cross-entropy (CE) loss, as the surrogate loss. But fairness-aware GNN models are trained with different loss functions for fairness, e.g., demographic parity loss, mutual information loss, and Wasserstein distance loss. The victim model is unknown and can be any type of fairness-aware GNN, so the attacker has to find a proper surrogate loss that represents the different types of loss functions of fairness-aware GNNs. (2) The attacks need to be unnoticeable. If the poisoned graph data shows any clues of being manipulated, the model owner could recognize them and take defensive actions, e.g., abandoning the poisoned input data. Usually attackers restrict the perturbation size so that the attacks are unnoticeable. We argue that in fairness attacks a distinct change of prediction utility can also be a strong clue of being manipulated. However, none of the existing works on fairness attacks has considered the unnoticeable utility change.

Because of these challenges, we propose a novel fairness attack method on GNNs called G-FairAttack. It has two parts: a carefully designed surrogate loss function and an optimization method. For the first challenge, we categorize existing fairness-aware GNNs into three types based on their fairness loss terms. Then we propose a novel surrogate loss function, with theoretical analysis, that helps the surrogate model learn from all types of fairness-aware GNNs. For the second challenge, we propose a novel unnoticeable constraint in utility change so that the fairness attack is unnoticeable. Then we propose a non-gradient attack algorithm to solve the constrained optimization problem, and it is verified to perform better than previous gradient-based methods. We also propose a fast computation strategy to make G-FairAttack more scalable. Our contributions are as follows.

- Attack Setting. We consider a novel unnoticeable constraint on prediction utility change for unnoticeable fairness attacks of GNNs. This can be extended to general fairness attacks.

- Objective Design. We propose a novel surrogate loss with theoretical analysis that helps the surrogate model learn from various types of fairness-aware GNNs.

- Algorithmic Design. We discuss the deficiency of previous gradient-based optimization methods and design a non-gradient attack method to solve the optimization problem with the unnoticeable constraint. We also propose a fast computation approach to reduce its time complexity.

- Experimental Evaluation. We conduct extensive experiments on three real-world datasets with four types of victim models, and they verify that G-FairAttack successfully jeopardizes the fairness of various fairness-aware GNNs while the effect on prediction utility is unnoticeable.

## Introduction

Despite that, many recent studies [10,11,12,13] have shown that GNNs could yield biased predictions for nodes from certain demographic groups (e.g., females). As GNNs become increasingly significant in high-stakes human-centered scenarios, addressing such prediction bias is imperative. Consequently, substantial efforts have been devoted to developing fairness-aware GNNs, which aim to learn fair node representations that can be used to make accurate and fair predictions. Typical strategies to improve the fairness of GNNs include adversarial training [14,10], regularization [15,16,17,18], and edge rewiring [19,20,21].

Although these fairness-aware GNN frameworks can make fair predictions, there remains a high risk that the exhibited fairness is corrupted by malicious attackers [22]. Adversarial attacks threaten the fairness of the victim model by perturbing the input graph data, which results in unfair predictions. Such fairness attacks can severely compromise the reliability of GNNs, even when they have a built-in fairness-enhancing mechanism. For instance, consider a GNN-based recommender system in social networks. In scenarios involving commercial competition or personal benefits, a malicious adversary might conduct fairness attacks by hijacking inactive user accounts. The adversary can collect user data from these accounts to train a fairness attack model, and then, according to the fairness attack algorithm, modify the attributes and connections of these compromised accounts. As a result, the GNN-based system is affected by the poisoned input data and makes biased predictions against a specific user group.

To protect the fairness of GNN models from adversarial attacks, we should first fully understand the potential ways to attack fairness. To this end, this paper investigates the problem of adversarial attacks on fairness of GNNs. Despite the importance of investigating fairness attacks on GNNs, most existing studies [23,24,25,26,27] only focus on attacking the utility of GNNs (e.g., prediction accuracy) and neglect their vulnerability in the fairness aspect. To study fairness attacks, we follow existing works of attacks on GNNs to formulate the attack as an optimization problem and consider the prevalent gray-box attack setting [23,24,28,29], where the attacker cannot access the architecture or parameters of the victim model [30,31]. A common strategy in gray-box attacks is to train a surrogate model [23,24] to gain more knowledge about the unseen victim model. Compared with conventional adversarial attacks, our attack on fairness is more difficult due to two challenges: (1) The design of the surrogate loss function. Previous attacks on prediction utility directly choose the loss function adopted by most victim models, i.e. the cross-entropy (CE) loss, as the surrogate loss. Because the victim model is unknown and can be any type of fairness-aware GNN, the attacker should find a proper surrogate loss that represents the different types of loss functions of fairness-aware GNNs. (2) The necessity of making such attacks unnoticeable. If the poisoned graph data exhibits any clues of manipulation, the model owner could recognize them and take defensive actions [23], e.g., abandoning the poisoned input data. Conventionally, attackers restrict the perturbation size to keep attacks unnoticeable. In fairness attacks, we argue that a distinct change of prediction utility can also be a strong clue of manipulation. However, none of the existing works on fairness attacks has considered an unnoticeable utility change.

In light of these challenges, we propose a novel fairness attack method on GNNs named G-FairAttack, which consists of two parts: a carefully designed surrogate loss function and an optimization method. To tackle the first challenge, we categorize existing fairness-aware GNNs into three types based on their fairness loss terms, and then propose a novel surrogate loss function, with theoretical analysis, to help the surrogate model learn from all types of fairness-aware GNNs. To address the second challenge, we propose a novel unnoticeable constraint in utility change to make the fairness attack unnoticeable. We then propose a non-gradient attack algorithm to solve the constrained optimization problem, which is verified to perform better than previous gradient-based methods. Moreover, we propose a fast computation strategy to improve the scalability of G-FairAttack. Our contributions are summarized as follows.

- • Attack Setting. We consider a novel unnoticeable constraint on prediction utility change for unnoticeable fairness attacks of GNNs, which can be extended to general fairness attacks.

- • Objective Design. We propose a novel surrogate loss with theoretical analysis to help the surrogate model learn from various types of fairness-aware GNNs.

- • Algorithmic Design. To solve the optimization problem with the unnoticeable constraint, we discuss the deficiency of previous gradient-based optimization methods and design a non-gradient attack method. We also propose a fast computation approach to reduce its time complexity.

- • Experimental Evaluation. We conduct extensive experiments on three real-world datasets with four types of victim models and verify that G-FairAttack successfully jeopardizes the fairness of various fairness-aware GNNs with an unnoticeable effect on prediction utility.
